title: Answering a Question With a Question
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes the case for "reverse questions" as a deliberate leadership tool for deepening conversations rather than deflecting them. It supplies a set of sample phrases leaders can use to bounce a question back to the asker for elaboration, and pairs these with reverse statements that similarly delay a direct answer to invite more reflection. The piece cautions that this technique only works when used sparingly and with genuine curiosity; overused, it reads as evasive or annoying. It closes by positioning the technique as a complement to, not a replacement for, giving direct answers.
points: Introduces "reverse questions" as a tool for deepening rather than deflecting dialogue
Provides sample phrasings leaders can use to redirect a question back to the asker
Warns that overuse makes the technique seem evasive or irritating
Positions the technique as a complement to direct answers, not a substitute
quotes: Answering a question with a question expands a conversation or discussion by sending the question back to the questioner for further exploration.
In order to clarify and understand more deeply what is being asked, the best leaders try hard to slow down and occasionally ask a question in reply.
When leaders defy this script and ask a question instead, everything changes.
The key is not to fill the silence with another question or statement too quickly.
Skillful leaders let the response linger before engaging the question or statement further.
Good leaders are ready with a question, as well as an answer to any query they receive.
